Sugar-containing goods are not covered (as now).
The bill, including the base period, was published on 2 March 2026, passed on 10 June 2026, and takes effect for the quota year beginning 1 January 2027 (ten months after it was proposed).
No expiry; the quota volume is reviewed in 2031.
Customs applies the rates; the Ministry of Trade's licence office keeps the register of quota shares and licences.

Importers of record pay a tariff of 2% ad valorem on imports of raw and white sugar covered by a licence, up to 400,000 t a year in total, and 60% ad valorem on all other sugar imports.
A licence covers raw or white sugar tonne for tonne.
Shares and licences may be sold or leased to any registered importer; transfers are registered with the licence office for a $200 fee.
Registration as an importer is open to any firm for $500.
Section 9: "A licence not used by 30 September of the quota year is surrendered."
Imports above a firm's licence pay the out-of-quota rate; misdeclaration is penalized as under existing customs law.
No expiry; the quota volume is reviewed in 2031.
The bill, including the base period, was published on 2 March 2026, passed on 10 June 2026, and takes effect for the quota year beginning 1 January 2027 (ten months after it was proposed).
Each firm that imported sugar in 2023 to 2025 receives a permanent share of the 400,000 t equal to its share of total imports in those years.
Each December, licences for the next year are issued to share holders pro rata.

context: Kestrany consumes about 1,750,000 tonnes (t) of sugar a year, about 60% by food and drink manufacturers and 40% by households.
Imports averaged about 650,000 t a year in 2023 to 2025: about 450,000 t of raw cane sugar refined at two port refineries in Vellport, and about 200,000 t of white sugar.
Kestrany takes about 1.2% of world sugar trade, bought from many exporters.
Under the existing flat 25% ad valorem tariff, white sugar lands at about $550 a tonne, which sets the domestic white price; tariff revenue is about $62.5 million a year.

Nine firms imported in 2023 to 2025: the two Vellport refiners (66% of imports), four trading houses (25%), and three manufacturers that import directly (a soft-drink bottler and two confectioners, 9%).

Kestrany's food manufacturers export about a fifth of their output, and imported confectionery, biscuits and soft-drink concentrates (not covered by the sugar tariff) hold about a quarter of the home market.
Two wet mills make glucose syrup from domestic maize.
The licence office's funding is not stated.
Existing rules that stay in the counterfactual: the flat 25% tariff on raw and white sugar; customs classification of sugar mixtures; the general budget, which receives the tariff.
